paras: The threatened lynching of Will Collins took place in Wilkinson County, Georgia, in April 1888, after Collins, a Black man, was accused of shooting and robbing J. A. Sheffield, a merchant of Irwinton. Townspeople tracked and captured him, and Sheriff Fountain took him to Macon to prevent a lynching. Collins was not harmed; in October 1888 a jury at Irwinton found him guilty of murder.

According to a Macon dispatch of April 30, Sheffield, described as "a prominent merchant at Irwinton," was on his way home on Saturday night, April 28, when he was killed with a shotgun by a man standing in the corner of a fence by the road. The dispatch named Collins as the gunman and said he then robbed Sheffield, stating both as fact. "The people of the town" turned out, tracked Collins from the scene and captured him.

On the morning of April 30 Sheriff Fountain of Wilkinson County arrived in Macon with Collins, who, the dispatch said, "was brought here to prevent lynching." The dispatch did not describe any crowd, gathering or threat against him beyond that phrase.

By late May Collins was held in the Bibb county jail, from which he wrote to Sheriff Fountain implicating another man. In the letter he said this man had paid him $20 on the afternoon before the murder to borrow his gun and shoes for an hour and had returned them that night. The sheriff placed "no confidence in the letter," reportedly because the man Collins named wore a size 10 shoe and Collins's shoes were 7s.

On October 5, 1888, an Irwinton dispatch reported that "William Collun," plainly the same defendant, had been found guilty of murder, in the second degree according to the full printed text, after the jury had been out twenty-four hours. No report of a sentence was found in the coverage.

The Macon wire ran on April 30 in the Washington Evening Star and the Alexandria Gazette and on May 1 in the Richmond Dispatch, the Richmond Daily Times and the Savannah Morning News. Its text was nearly identical everywhere, but editors framed it differently: the Alexandria Gazette headed it simply "Captured," the Savannah paper "A Wilkinson County Crime," while the Evening Star used "To Save Collins from Lynching" and the Richmond Daily Times "Threatened to Lynch Him." The Richmond Dispatch, under "Saved from Lynching," spelled the names "Sheifield" and "Fontaine."

Each version identified Collins as "the negro" and treated his guilt as settled before any trial. The Savannah Morning News alone followed the case afterward, in short Georgia items that again called Collins the man "who murdered" Sheffield, once giving the victim's initials as "J. H."

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Will Collins
bases: Collins, accused of murder and captured by townspeople, was removed from Wilkinson County by the sheriff 'to prevent lynching'; no mob action against him is reported, so this is a threatened lynching (A1, A2, A5).

Collins was not killed: he was taken to Macon to prevent lynching, held in the Bibb county jail, and later tried and convicted (A1, A6, A7). No group is reported to have acted against him beyond the wire's phrase about preventing a lynching.

The capture and the lynching danger rest on one Macon wire story reprinted in five papers (A1-A5); the separate Savannah items corroborate the murder charge, jailing and conviction but say nothing of a mob (A6, A7).

accounts.label: Macon wire report
accounts.gist: Collins shot Sheffield from a fence corner and robbed him; townspeople tracked and captured him, and the sheriff brought him to Macon to prevent lynching.

accounts.label: Collins's letter
accounts.gist: Collins wrote that another man paid him $20 the afternoon before the murder to borrow his gun and shoes, returning them that night; the sheriff rejected it because the man wore size 10 shoes and Collins's were 7s.

framing.detail: The Macon wire, presenting Collins's guilt as fact, ran in Washington, Alexandria, Richmond and Savannah papers with headlines from 'Captured' to 'Threatened to Lynch Him'.
The Savannah Morning News followed the case in brief Georgia items on Collins's letter and his conviction, both calling him the man 'who murdered' Sheffield.

conflicts.note: The wire and the trial report agree on 'J. A.'; 'J. H.' in a single column item is likely an error.
'Collun' in the conviction item is most likely OCR or typesetting for Collins; same victim and date.

record_check.dossier: The threatened target was Will Collins; Sheffield was the man Collins was accused of killing, not a target of mob violence.
Black: Collins is called 'the negro Will Collins'.
threatened: the only evidence is that he was moved 'to prevent lynching'; no attempt on him is reported.
Pursuit and capture by townspeople, removal by the sheriff; the killing was the murder Collins was accused of, not an act against him.
Captured by townspeople and held by the sheriff, who took him to Macon.
One death, Sheffield's, from the alleged murder; no one was killed by a mob.

record_check.record: ...the sheriff took him to Macon to prevent lynching.
record_check.dossier: Add: Collins was held in the Bibb county jail and convicted of murder (second degree per page OCR) at Irwinton on Oct 5, 1888.
